title: Feedback Loops & Honest Mirrors
hook: Everyone around you can see your face except you, and almost none of them will tell you the truth about it unless you make it safe to.
why:
A head chef loses three good cooks in a year. Each one gives a different reason for leaving, a better offer, a move, a shorter commute, and each reason is true enough. Nobody mentions what all three experienced every night at the pass: the chef going silent, staring at a plate and then at the cook, in a way that felt like an explosion about to happen. The chef has no idea. He thinks of himself as demanding but fair, and nobody has ever told him otherwise, because nobody tells the head chef anything.

The previous chapter gave you a camera. This one gives you something a camera cannot: the view of people who see you every day, in settings you cannot record, over months rather than minutes. That view exists already. It is simply locked behind politeness, power and fear. This chapter is about getting it out honestly, receiving it without flinching, and using it to close the gap between how you think you come across and how you do.

teach.h: Other people know things about you that you cannot know yourself.
teach.p:
In 1955 the psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham drew a simple four-pane window to describe what is known about a person. One pane holds what both you and others know; one, what you know and others do not; one, what nobody yet knows. The fourth holds what others can see and you cannot: your blind spot. For a reader of bodies, almost everything about your own nonverbal behaviour sits in that fourth pane.

Later research has given the window some numbers. Simine Vazire's self-other knowledge asymmetry model, tested in 2010, found that people tend to be the better judges of their own inner states, such as how anxious they feel, while the people who know them are often better judges of traits that are visible from outside or loaded with evaluation, the kind of thing that shows in how a person comes across. Neither side has the whole picture. Each sees what the other cannot.

This is not a claim that other people are always right about you. Friends misread you, colleagues project their own preoccupations, and a single opinion can be wildly off. It is a claim about where certain information lives. If you want to know how your face looks when you listen, the person sitting across from you has better data than you do.

Seen this way, asking for feedback is not humility or self-doubt. It is simply going to the source that holds the evidence, the same way you would consult a baseline journal rather than your memory.
teach.disconfirm: If the people who know you best consistently describe you in ways that surprise you not at all, your blind pane may be small. Before concluding that, check whether you have ever asked them a question specific enough to be surprised by.

teach.h: Most feedback is filtered out before it reaches you.
teach.p:
In 1970 Sidney Rosen and Abraham Tesser described what they called the MUM effect: people are reluctant to pass on bad news, even when it is not their fault and even when the recipient needs it. They delay, soften, or simply say nothing. Ask almost anyone whether they have ever told a friend he has bad breath, or told a boss he comes across as frightening, and you will see the effect at work.

Power makes it stronger. The more senior you are, the more people depend on your goodwill, and the less they will risk telling you something unwelcome about yourself. Managers, fathers, older brothers, team captains and anyone with a temper are routinely the last to know how they come across. Silence around a powerful person is not evidence of approval. It is often evidence of caution.

Culture and setting shape the filter too. In some workplaces direct criticism is a sign of respect; in others it is an insult. Some families tease each other about everything except the things that actually matter. Men, in many settings, are given especially little honest feedback about how they make others feel, partly because they are expected not to want it.

The practical conclusion is uncomfortable: the absence of complaints tells you very little. If you have never heard criticism of how you come across, the most likely explanation is not that there is nothing to criticise. It is that nobody has found it safe or worthwhile to say.
teach.disconfirm: If people who depend on you regularly volunteer uncomfortable observations without being asked, your filter is unusually thin, and the silence you meet elsewhere may mean what it seems to. That is rare enough to check rather than assume.

teach.h: Ask for something specific, observable and small.
teach.p:
*How do I come across?* is the worst possible question. It is vague, it asks for a judgment about your whole personality, and it invites the safest possible answer, which is *fine*. Most people asked it will say something kind and change the subject.

Good questions are specific, observable and small. *When I'm listening in our meetings, what does my face do?* *When I disagree with someone, what do you notice first?* *Is there one habit of mine that might be misread by people who don't know me?* Each asks about behaviour the other person could have seen, in a particular setting, and each asks for one thing rather than a verdict.

The organisational psychologist Tasha Eurich, in her work on self-awareness, recommends asking *what* rather than *why*. Why do people find me intimidating invites speculation about your character. What do I do that might feel intimidating invites a description of behaviour, which is useful, actionable and far less painful to give.

Make the question easier to answer honestly. Ask in private, not in front of others. Give the person time: *have a think, and tell me next week*. Say explicitly that you want the honest version and that there will be no comeback, and then make sure there is none. And ask for an example: *can you remember a time I did that?* An example turns an impression into something you can check against your journal or a recording.

Timing matters as much as wording. Do not ask in the middle of a disagreement, straight after a bad day, or when the other person is busy; the answer will be shaped by the moment. Ask on an ordinary day, about an ordinary setting, and you will hear about your ordinary habits, which are the ones people actually live with.
teach.disconfirm: If your specific questions keep getting vague answers, the difficulty may not be the question but the safety. Ask someone with less to lose, or ask the same person again after showing that the first answer cost them nothing.

teach.h: Choose mirrors who see you often, wish you well, and lose nothing by honesty.
teach.p:
Not everyone is a good mirror. The best ones meet three conditions. They see you often, in the setting you care about, so their view is based on many observations rather than one memorable evening. They wish you well, so their feedback is aimed at helping you rather than scoring a point. And they have little to lose by being honest, which usually means they do not depend on you for their job, their money or their peace at home.

Those conditions rule out more people than you might think. Your manager sees you often but may have reasons to shade the truth. Your partner wishes you well but may not see you at work, and may have good reasons not to criticise you. An admiring junior colleague will flatter you; a rival will find fault. None of these people is useless, but none should be your only mirror.

Aim for two or three mirrors in different settings: one at work, one among friends, one in your family or wherever else you spend your life. A peer at work, an old friend who has known you for years, a sibling who has no reason to be polite. Where their observations agree, you have found something real. Where they differ, you may have found the way you change between settings, which is itself worth knowing.

Treat the relationship as reciprocal where you can. Offer to be an honest mirror in return. People are far more willing to tell you the truth when they know you will do the same for them, and do it kindly.
teach.disconfirm: If your mirrors from different settings describe you in ways that never overlap, either you behave very differently in each, or at least one of them is not seeing you clearly. Ask each for an example before deciding which.

teach.h: Receive it without defending, explaining or fixing on the spot.
teach.p:
Feedback about how you come across tends to land in the body before the mind. A flush, a tightening jaw, arms folding, a sudden urge to explain. By now you should recognise these as your own pacifiers and strain signals, and the moment you notice them is the moment to slow down.

Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen, in their book on receiving feedback, describe three triggers that make people reject it. Truth triggers: the feedback seems wrong. Relationship triggers: you resent who is giving it, or how. Identity triggers: it threatens your sense of who you are. Each is understandable, and each makes you argue with information you asked for.

The discipline is simple to describe and hard to do. Thank the person. Ask one clarifying question, usually for an example. Do not defend, explain your intentions, or promise to change, not yet. Write down what they said, word for word, as soon as you can. Understanding feedback is a separate act from agreeing with it, and agreeing is a separate act from deciding what to do.

There is a practical reason for this beyond politeness. If you argue with the first honest thing someone tells you, they will never tell you another. The way you receive the first piece of feedback decides whether there will be a second.

Use what you know about your own body while you listen. Breathe out slowly, let your hands rest, uncross your arms if they have crossed. These are not tricks to look receptive; they lower your own arousal enough to hear the words rather than the threat. A man whose shoulders are up around his ears is listening to his own alarm, not to the person in front of him.
teach.disconfirm: If, after a few days, you still disagree with the feedback after checking it against a recording or another mirror, you may be right to set it aside. The point is to decide later, with evidence, not in the first heated seconds.
teach.pullQuote: The way you receive the first piece of feedback decides whether there will be a second.

teach.h: Feedback can make things worse; aim it at the behaviour, not the person.
teach.p:
It is tempting to assume that more feedback is always better. In 1996 Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi pooled several hundred studies of feedback interventions and found something surprising: feedback improved performance on average, but in more than a third of cases it made performance worse. One pattern stood out. Feedback that drew attention to the person, their worth or their character, tended to do harm; feedback that kept attention on the task tended to help.

The lesson applies in both directions. When you receive feedback, translate it toward behaviour. *You're intimidating* becomes *when I stand over people's desks while they work, they feel watched*. The first is a verdict on who you are; the second is a habit you can change.

When you give feedback, which you will once people learn you take it well, start from behaviour and stay there. Describe what you saw and when, the way you would write it in your journal, and leave the person's character out of it. *In the meeting, you looked at your phone each time Sarah spoke* is something a colleague can use. *You don't respect her* is something he can only defend against.

Feedback about nonverbal behaviour is especially easy to turn into a verdict, because bodies feel like the self. Keep the description close to what a camera could have recorded, and it stays useful.

Be alert, too, to feedback that repeats body-language myths. *You crossed your arms, so you were being defensive* is a reading from a gesture dictionary, not an observation. Thank the person, keep the description and discard the dictionary: you crossed your arms in that meeting, and the question of why belongs to your baseline, not to a list of meanings.
teach.disconfirm: If you find feedback about your behaviour makes you feel worse about yourself without suggesting anything to change, it has probably drifted toward your character. Ask for the specific behaviour behind it before deciding what it means.

teach.h: Close the loop: act, check, and report back.
teach.p:
A loop that is never closed is not a loop. After receiving feedback, decide whether to act on it, and if so, choose one small change, the same way you would after a video review. Try it for a couple of weeks.

Then go back to the same person and ask: *a few weeks ago you mentioned I look at my laptop when people are talking. I've been trying to stop. Have you noticed any difference?* This does three things. It tells you whether the change is visible from outside. It tells the person their honesty was heard and used, which makes them more willing to be honest again. And it often brings a second, finer piece of feedback that the first conversation could not have produced.

If you decide not to act on a piece of feedback, it is often worth saying so, kindly. *I thought about what you said about my tone with the team. I'm going to keep being direct with them, but I wanted you to know I took it seriously.* People can accept disagreement far more easily than they can accept being ignored.

Keep a short record of each loop in your journal: what you heard, what you changed, what you heard back. Over a year, that record becomes a map of how other people experience you and how that has changed, which is more than most people ever have.

Do not overuse your mirrors. Asking the same person for feedback every week turns a gift into a burden, and it can start to look like a need for reassurance. Once a month per mirror, at most, is plenty. Between conversations, the camera, the journal and your own attention can do most of the checking.
teach.disconfirm: If people you return to say they have noticed no change, either the change was not visible or it did not last. Check a recording before concluding that the feedback was wrong in the first place.

poseGallery.doCaption: Hearing it leaning in, asking for one example.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hearing feedback with arms locked, preparing a defence.
poseGallery.annotation: Your own strain signals arrive first. Notice them, slow down, and understand before you agree or disagree.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Asking 'how do I come across?' and hearing 'fine'.
poseGallery.annotation: Specific, observable, small. A question about behaviour in one setting gets an answer you can use.

poseGallery.doCaption: Nodding, thanking, and taking it away to think.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Explaining why the feedback is wrong, on the spot.

poseGallery.doCaption: Taking it as information about one habit.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking criticism as a verdict on who you are.

One view can be as distorted as none. Check it against mirrors from other settings before you change.

caseStudy:
Luis, thirty-six, is head chef of a busy restaurant. In a year he has lost three good line cooks. Each gave a reasonable reason for leaving, and Luis believes them. His owner, less convinced, suggests he ask someone.

Luis chooses two mirrors: his sous-chef, Ana, who works beside him every night and is planning to open her own place within a year, and the front-of-house manager, Kemal, who watches the kitchen through the pass and does not report to him. He asks each the same question, privately, after service: *When I'm checking plates at the pass, what does my face do? Take a few days if you like. I want the honest version, and nothing you say will come back on you.*

Kemal answers the next night. *You go completely silent. You stare at the plate, then you stare at whoever cooked it. You don't say anything for a few seconds, even when the plate is fine. The young ones think you're about to explode.* Ana, a day later, gives an example: a Saturday when a cook burned his hand because he was watching Luis instead of the pan.

Luis feels his face go hot and wants to explain that he is only concentrating. Instead he thanks them both and writes down exactly what they said. He records his own face at the pass on two quiet nights. The silence is there, and the stare, and it does look like rage.

He chooses one change: within two seconds of picking up a plate he says something, *good*, or one specific fix. Three weeks later he asks Kemal whether he has noticed anything. Kemal says the young cooks have stopped looking at the pass while they work. Ana adds that he still stares at the sauce station, which is where the next conversation starts.

At a group meeting that spring, a chef from the company's other restaurant asks his own team whether he is too harsh. They say no, chef. He loses two more cooks by summer.
observe: This week, notice one moment when someone seemed to hold back a comment about you, such as a pause, a laugh or a never mind, and write down what had just happened.
Ask one person who sees you often a single specific question about one observable habit, and write their answer down word for word before you respond.
At work or at home, notice who tells you uncomfortable things and who never does, and list the two groups privately in your journal.

drills.name: Write the Question
steps: Write down five questions you might ask someone about how you come across, in your own words.
Mark each as vague, personal or behavioural.
Rewrite each vague or personal question so that it asks about one observable behaviour in one setting.
Add a request for an example to each.
Choose the one you would be most nervous to ask, and keep it for this week.
variations: Ask a trusted friend to rate your rewritten questions as vague, personal or behavioural, and see whether they agree with you.
Write one question about how you come across at home as well as at work.
Turn one of your questions into a question about a single meeting or event, so that the answer can be checked against a recording.

drills.name: Choose Your Mirrors
steps: List everyone who sees you regularly in the settings you care about.
Rate each from one to three on how often they see you, how much they wish you well, and how little they lose by being honest.
Cross out anyone who scores one on the third measure.
Choose two or three mirrors from different settings among the highest scorers.
Write one line on what you could offer each of them in return.
variations: Add a fourth measure to your list: how different the person's experience of you is likely to be from your own.
Choose one mirror you would never normally ask, such as someone much younger or older, and consider whether they meet the three conditions.
Check whether all your chosen mirrors see you in the same setting, and replace one if they do.

drills.name: Receiving Rehearsal
steps: Recall a piece of criticism about yourself that you argued with or dismissed.
Write down, as honestly as you can, what you said and what your body did.
Rewrite your response as three parts: thanks, one clarifying question, and silence.
Say the rewritten response aloud three times, noticing where your body wants to defend.
Note which of Stone and Heen's three triggers that criticism touched: truth, relationship or identity.
variations: Rehearse your three-part response with a friend who delivers a mildly unfair piece of criticism, so that you practise under some pressure.
Write down what your body does in the first second of hearing criticism, and use that as your cue to slow down.
Recall a piece of praise you deflected, and rehearse receiving it with a simple thank you.

drills.name: Task, Not Self
steps: Write down three pieces of feedback you have given other people in the past year.
Mark any part that described their character rather than something they did.
Rewrite each as a description a camera could have recorded, with when it happened.
Read the original and the rewrite aloud, imagining you are on the receiving end.
Note which version you would rather hear.
variations: Rewrite one piece of feedback you received in the past, as you would have wanted to receive it, in camera language.
Notice the next time someone gives feedback about a person rather than a task, and how the recipient responds.
Practise giving one piece of positive feedback in camera language, which is often more useful than general praise.

drills.name: Close the Loop
steps: Choose one piece of feedback you received in the past month and decided to act on.
Write the one small change you made, or will make, in a single sentence.
Put a date in your calendar two weeks from now to ask the same person about it.
Write out the exact words you will use to ask.
After asking, add what you heard to your journal under the original feedback.
variations: Close the loop on a piece of feedback from more than a year ago, if you can, and ask whether the change has lasted.
Write down what you will do if the person says they have not noticed any difference.
Tell the person, when you close the loop, one specific thing their feedback helped you understand.

quiz.q: Nobody at work has ever told you that you come across as impatient. What can you conclude?
options: That you do not come across as impatient, since someone would have mentioned it by now
That your colleagues are unobservant, or too busy with their own work to notice you
Very little: people withhold unwelcome feedback, especially from someone with power over them
That you should ask your manager to confirm it, since managers see the most of you
quiz.explain: Rosen and Tesser's MUM effect describes how reluctant people are to pass on bad news, and power makes them more reluctant still. Silence around a senior person is often caution, not approval. The only way to find out is to ask in a way that makes honesty safe.

quiz.q: What did Vazire's self-other knowledge asymmetry research suggest about who knows what about a person?
options: Others often judge visible traits well, while people often know their own inner states, such as anxiety, better
People always know themselves best in every respect, since only they have direct access to their own thoughts and feelings
Strangers know you better than friends do, because they have no history to bias their judgment
Self-knowledge and other people's knowledge of you turn out to be much the same in every area
quiz.explain: Each side sees what the other cannot. Your inner experience is yours; how you come across is visible to the people around you. Asking for feedback means going to the source that holds the evidence.

quiz.q: You ask your sister how you come across with your children, and she says you can be a bit sharp with them. You feel your face go hot. What is the best next move?
options: Explain that you are only firm with them because you care about them
Point out, gently, that she is not a parent herself and cannot know
Change the subject for now, and think it over later on your own
Thank her and ask for one recent example of when she saw it
quiz.explain: Thanks and a request for an example keep the door open and turn an impression into something you can check. Explaining or attacking her standing triggers exactly the defence Stone and Heen describe, and it guarantees she will not tell you anything again.

quiz.q: What did Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis of feedback interventions find?
options: Feedback improves performance in almost every case, as long as it is given promptly
It helped on average, but in over a third of cases made things worse, especially when aimed at the person
Negative feedback is nearly always harmful, while positive feedback nearly always helps
Feedback only works when it comes from a manager or someone else with authority
quiz.explain: More feedback is not automatically better. What it draws attention to matters: the task and the behaviour tend to help, the self tends to harm. That is why this chapter translates every piece of feedback toward behaviour.

quiz.q: Who makes the best honest mirror?
options: Someone who always tells you that you are doing well, so you stay motivated
Your harshest critic, because they hold nothing back and will spare you nothing
Someone who sees you often, wishes you well, and loses little by being honest
Your manager, because they see you most often and know your work the best
quiz.explain: Frequency gives the mirror enough observations, goodwill aims the feedback at helping you, and having little to lose makes honesty possible. An admirer or a critic alone gives you a distorted picture, and a manager may have reasons to shade the truth.

quiz.q: Two weeks after changing how you listen in meetings, what closes the feedback loop?
options: Going back to the person who raised it, asking if they have noticed a difference, and saying what you tried
Assuming the change has worked if nobody complains about your listening in the next month
Asking the whole team in a meeting whether your listening has improved since you last asked
Recording the next meeting without telling anyone, and then checking the recording carefully for any sign of change
quiz.explain: Returning to the same person tells you whether the change is visible and shows them their honesty was used. It often brings a second, finer piece of feedback. Silence, as this chapter showed, tells you very little.

quiz.q: What did Rosen and Tesser's MUM effect, described in 1970, refer to?
options: People's tendency to pass on good news quickly and loudly to everyone around them
People's reluctance to pass on bad news, even when the recipient needs to hear it
People's habit of mumbling when they are nervous about speaking to someone senior
People's preference for receiving feedback from their mothers rather than colleagues
quiz.explain: People delay, soften or say nothing when the news is unwelcome, even when it is not their fault and the recipient needs it. Power makes the effect stronger.

quiz.q: Your mother says you come across as arrogant, but two colleagues and a client, asked separately, say you are direct and sometimes impatient. What fits this chapter best?
options: Reshape yourself around your mother's view, since she knows you best of all
Weigh all four views, note the setting each comes from, and work on the shared point
Dismiss all the feedback, since the different mirrors cannot agree with each other
Ask your mother again until she agrees with the others about how you come across
quiz.explain: One mirror can be as distorted as none, and each sees you in a particular setting. Several mirrors from different settings, and the point on which they agree, are the most reliable guide to what to change.

quiz.q: Someone says that the more senior you become, the more honest feedback you receive, because people respect you. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That power strengthens the reluctance to deliver bad news, so senior people often hear less
That senior people always receive more honest feedback, because they are trusted by everyone
That seniority makes no difference to feedback, since people are equally honest with everyone
That only junior people need feedback, so seniority makes feedback unnecessary in any case
quiz.explain: The more people depend on your goodwill, the more they risk by being honest, which strengthens the MUM effect. Senior people often have to work hardest to hear the truth.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific occasion when someone told you something uncomfortable about how you come across. What exactly did they say, in their words if you can remember them? What did your body do as you heard it, and what did you say back? Looking at it now, which part of what they said was about something they could see and you could not? And did you ever go back to them?
reflection.guidance: Most men can remember at least one piece of feedback that stung, and most remember their own defence more vividly than the feedback itself. Try to separate the two. Write their words first, then your reaction, then what you said. Be honest about the reaction; this is where you will see which of the three triggers was touched. If you never went back to that person, consider whether it is still possible. A late *I've been thinking about what you said* is far better than none.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to ask for feedback while really asking for reassurance. The reader asks *how do I come across?* to people who will say *fine*, hears *fine*, and concludes he has no blind spots. A second failure is to collect feedback and argue with it, which teaches every mirror he has to stop being honest. A third is to collect feedback and never act on it or return to the people who gave it, so that it becomes a ritual rather than a loop. A quieter failure is to treat one person's view as the truth and reshape yourself around it, when one mirror can be as distorted as none. Ask specific questions of two or three people in different settings, receive what they say with thanks, check it against a recording, change one thing, and go back.

furtherStudy.work: Thanks for the Feedback: The Science and Art of Receiving Feedback Well
furtherStudy.author: Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen
furtherStudy.note: The source of the three triggers, and the most practical book on receiving criticism.

furtherStudy.work: The effects of feedback interventions on performance
furtherStudy.author: Avraham N. Kluger and Angelo DeNisi
furtherStudy.note: Psychological Bulletin 119(2), 1996. The meta-analysis showing that feedback can make things worse.

furtherStudy.work: Who knows what about a person? The self-other knowledge asymmetry (SOKA) model
furtherStudy.author: Simine Vazire
furtherStudy.note: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 98(2), 2010.

furtherStudy.author: Tasha Eurich
furtherStudy.note: On internal and external self-awareness, and why asking what works better than asking why.

moreCases.title: The vicar who asked how it went
moreCases.scene:
Tim, fifty-one, has been vicar of a market-town parish for two years. Every Sunday, at the door after the service, he asks people how they found the sermon. Every Sunday, they say it was lovely, thought-provoking or just what they needed to hear. Attendance, meanwhile, has been falling slowly, and the younger families who came at Christmas have not come back.

His wife, Clare, suggests that "How did you find it?" at the church door, with a queue behind, is not a question anyone can answer honestly. Tim is sceptical, but he tries something different. He chooses two people: Margaret, a churchwarden of thirty years who sits near the front and has no reason to flatter him, and Josh, twenty-four, a youth worker who sits at the back. He asks each of them, privately, during the week: "When I'm preaching, where do my eyes go, and what do I do with my hands? Take a few days. I'd really like the honest version."

Margaret answers on Wednesday. She says, gently, that he preaches entirely to the left side of the church, where the choir and the older congregation sit, and that he reads from his notes almost the whole time. Josh says that from the back, Tim looks as though he is talking to himself, and that the families on the right-hand side have started sitting there because they feel nobody will notice if the children fidget.

Tim had no idea.

He also realises, thinking about it, that he has never once been told anything critical about his preaching in two years, and that he had taken that as a good sign.

He also notices, now that he is looking, that people leaving by the right-hand door at the end of the service rarely stop to shake his hand.
moreCases.misread:
Tim read the congregation's "lovely" at the door as feedback, and the falling attendance as a mystery. The congregation had been telling him what was kind to say, because his question gave them no room to say anything else.

And Tim read his own question as an invitation to honesty, when, asked at the door with a queue behind, it was an invitation to be polite.

The families on the right-hand side, for their part, had read his preaching to the left as a sign that the church was for the older congregation, and had begun to drift away without ever saying so.
moreCases.betterRead:
Rosen and Tesser described the MUM effect: people are reluctant to pass on bad news, and they soften it or say nothing, especially to someone in a position of authority. "How did you find it?" asked at the door is vague, public and personal, and it invites the safest answer, as this chapter explains. Tim's better approach was the one the chapter recommends: a specific, observable question, asked privately, of mirrors who saw him often, wished him well and had little to lose by honesty. He also chose them from different parts of the church, which gave him two views of the same habit. He changed one thing: he moved to the centre of the chancel and spoke the first and last paragraph of each sermon from memory, looking at the whole church. A month later, he asked Margaret and Josh again. Both said they had noticed. By Easter, two of the younger families were back.

He also stopped asking about the sermon at the door, and asked people about their week instead, which several of them said they preferred.

moreCases.title: The manager who argued with feedback
moreCases.scene:
Leanne, forty-four, is an operations manager at a logistics firm, and she prides herself on being open to feedback. At her annual 360 review, one comment stands out: "Leanne can be intimidating in meetings; people are reluctant to raise problems." She is hurt and irritated. At the next team meeting, she reads the comment out and says that she wants to understand it, because she has always tried to be approachable.

There is silence. Then one of her team leaders, Dean, says, carefully, that sometimes when people bring problems, she interrupts before they have finished. Leanne says that she interrupts because she is trying to help them get to the point faster, which is not the same as being intimidating. Another team leader says that she sometimes frowns when people disagree with her. Leanne says that she frowns when she is thinking, and that she cannot help her face. A third person says nothing.

The meeting moves on. Over the following months, the 360 comments become shorter and blander. The next year, nobody mentions intimidation at all. Leanne takes this as a sign that the problem has gone away.

Her director, Rob, notices that her team's incident reports have dropped by a third, while incidents logged by the safety team have not.

She also notices, though she does not connect it at the time, that Dean stops speaking in the next two meetings.
moreCases.misread:
Leanne read the original comment as unfair and the follow-up comments in the meeting as misunderstandings she needed to correct. Her team read her explanations as a clear message that honest feedback would be argued with, and stopped giving it.

Rob, her director, had also read the quieter 360s as improvement, until the incident figures told a different story.

She also read the blander 360 comments the following year as evidence that she had changed, when the only thing that had changed was what her team was willing to write.
moreCases.betterRead:
Stone and Heen describe three triggers that make people reject feedback: truth triggers, when it seems wrong; relationship triggers, when you resent who is giving it; and identity triggers, when it threatens your sense of who you are. Leanne's sense of herself as approachable was an identity trigger, and each explanation she gave taught her mirrors to stop being honest, which this chapter names as a common failure. The drop in incident reports was the cost. Her better approach, which Rob coached her through, was the Receiving Rehearsal: thanks, one clarifying question, a commitment to think about it, and nothing else. She went back to Dean and said, "You were right, and I argued instead of listening. Can you tell me what the interrupting looks like from your side?" She changed one habit: letting people finish. Incident reports rose again within two months.

She also asked Rob to tell her, privately, if he ever saw her arguing with feedback again, which he did twice that year.

moreCases.title: The coach who said soft
moreCases.scene:
Mick, fifty-eight, has coached amateur boxing at a community club for twenty years, and his feedback is famous. When a young boxer drops his guard in sparring, Mick shouts, "You're soft! Hands up!" When someone loses a bout, he tells them they did not want it enough. He believes that boxers need to hear the truth.

One of his most talented young boxers, Kayden, seventeen, has started to lose bouts he should win. After each loss, Mick tells him that he lacks heart. Kayden's sparring gets worse. He starts flinching before punches land and stops coming to Thursday sessions.

A new assistant coach, Leah, thirty, who has a background in sports science, watches a sparring session with Mick and notices that Kayden's guard drops in a specific moment: when he is tired, at the end of the second round, and always after throwing a right hand. She suggests to Mick that they tell Kayden that, rather than that he is soft.

Mick is sceptical. He has always told boxers what he thinks of them. But he agrees to let Leah try.

Kayden's mother has also noticed that he comes home from training quiet and goes straight to his room, and has asked Mick whether something has happened. Mick told her that the boy needs toughening up.

Leah also notices that the other young boxers have started to drop their eyes when Mick walks past, and that the club's membership has fallen by a quarter in two years.

Mick, watching Leah's video, sees the dropped guard for the first time, after twenty years of shouting about heart.
moreCases.misread:
Mick read Kayden's dropped guard and lost bouts as a lack of heart, and told him so, as feedback about who Kayden was. Kayden read the feedback as a verdict on himself, and his performance got worse as a result.

Kayden's mother read his withdrawal as a sign that he was being bullied, which was closer to the truth than Mick realised.

And Mick read his own bluntness as honesty, the thing he believed boxers most needed, when the honesty that helps is about the task, not the person.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kluger and DeNisi pooled several hundred studies of feedback and found that in more than a third of cases it made performance worse, and that feedback drawing attention to the person rather than the task tended to do harm. "You're soft" is feedback about the self; "your guard drops after your right hand when you're tired" is feedback about the task, which a boxer can act on. Leah's better approach was the Task, Not Self drill: describe what a camera would have recorded, with when and after what. She showed Kayden a phone video of the moment, and they practised returning the right hand to his chin at the end of tiring rounds. Within a month, Kayden won his next bout. Mick, watching, said nothing for a while, and then asked Leah to show him how she had filmed it.

Kayden also started coming back on Thursdays. When Mick later asked him what had changed, he said it was the first time anyone had told him something he could actually fix, instead of something about himself he could not.

moreCases.title: The consultant who listened to one mirror
moreCases.scene:
Rajesh, thirty-three, is an IT consultant, and after reading this chapter he decides to ask for feedback about how he comes across. He asks his mother, with whom he is very close and who has always been frank with him. She says, immediately, that he can come across as arrogant: he talks over people, he corrects them and he does not listen. Rajesh is shaken. He takes it to heart.

Over the next two months he reshapes himself. In client meetings he speaks less, defers to everyone, prefaces his recommendations with "I might be wrong, but", and avoids correcting anyone, even when they are mistaken. He holds back his hands and keeps his voice soft.

A client, Deborah, rings his manager to say that Rajesh seems unsure of his own advice and that she is no longer confident in his recommendations. His manager, Paul, is surprised, and asks Rajesh what has changed.

Rajesh explains. Paul says that he has never once found Rajesh arrogant at work, and suggests that Rajesh ask two or three more people, in different settings, before reshaping himself any further.

He also notices that he has started apologising before he speaks, even with friends, and that his girlfriend has asked him whether something is wrong.

In one meeting, he lets a client's colleague give a wrong figure to the board without correcting it, because he is afraid of seeming arrogant, and the mistake costs the client a week.
moreCases.misread:
Rajesh read his mother's view as the truth about how he came across everywhere, and reshaped himself around it. His client read the reshaped Rajesh, hesitant and deferential, as a consultant who did not believe his own advice.

Rajesh also read his mother's honesty as accuracy, which is an easy mistake to make with someone who loves you and has never lied to you.

His mother, for her part, had been describing the son who argued with his brothers over dinner, not the consultant his clients knew, and would have been surprised to learn how seriously he had taken it.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter warns that one person's view can be as distorted as none, and that the best mirrors see you often in the setting you care about, wish you well and lose nothing by honesty. Rajesh's mother met two of those conditions, but she saw him mostly at family dinners, arguing with his brothers, which is a very different setting from a client meeting. Vazire's work suggests that others know things about us that we cannot see, but which others, and in which settings, matters. Paul's better advice was the Choose Your Mirrors drill: two or three mirrors from different settings. Rajesh asked Paul, a colleague and a long-standing client. All three said he was direct and occasionally impatient when a client misunderstood a technical point, but not arrogant. He kept his directness, worked on his patience and stopped saying "I might be wrong" when he was not.

He also thanked his mother, and told her that she was right about family dinners, which made her laugh.

workedReading.title: Asking for feedback as a new team lead
workedReading.scene:
Ayesha, thirty-two, was promoted three months ago to lead a team of eight software engineers, several of whom were her peers until recently. She suspects that something about how she comes across has changed since the promotion: the team chats less when she joins them, and two people have stopped bringing her problems early. Nobody has said anything. She knows from this chapter that, as their manager, she is now the person least likely to be told the truth, because power strengthens the MUM effect. She decides to build a feedback loop deliberately, and to do it in the way the chapter recommends: specific questions, chosen mirrors, a receiving response she has rehearsed, a check against a recording and a return visit.

She also knows that, three months ago, she would have been one of the people telling her old manager what they really thought, and that she is now on the other side of that conversation.

steps.label: Choose your mirrors
steps.text:
She uses the Choose Your Mirrors drill. She lists everyone who sees her at work and rates them on how often they see her, how much they wish her well, and how little they lose by honesty. She chooses three: Tom, a senior engineer who is leaving for a new job in two months; Grace, a product manager from another team who sits in her stand-ups; and her own former manager, who now works in a different department.

She also notes that none of the three report to her, which is part of what makes them safe to be honest.

She also writes, next to each name, what she can offer in return, such as a reference for Tom or help with Grace's next project.

steps.label: Write the question
steps.text:
She writes a question that is specific, observable and small, as the Write the Question drill suggests: "When someone brings me a problem in our stand-ups, what does my face or body do in the first few seconds?" She adds a request for an example. She avoids "How am I doing as a manager?", which would invite reassurance.

She also writes a second question, to use only if the first produces nothing: "Is there one habit of mine that might be misread by people who don't know me well?"

She also tests the question on a friend outside work first, to check that it is clear and does not sound like fishing.

steps.label: Ask privately, and give time
steps.text:
She asks each of them in person, one to one, and says: "Take a few days if you like. I'd really like the honest version, and nothing you say will come back on you." She means the last sentence, and she knows she will have to show it. She asks them not to answer straight away, because a considered answer is usually more specific.

She also resists the urge to ask her direct reports, who would face the strongest version of the MUM effect.

steps.label: Receive without defending
steps.text:
Tom answers first. He says that when someone raises a problem, she sighs, very slightly, and looks at her laptop before they have finished. Ayesha feels her face flush and an urge to explain that she sighs because she is tired. She notices the urge, as the chapter suggests, says "Thank you, that's really useful. Can you remember an example?" and listens. Tom gives one from the previous Tuesday.

She also writes down Tom's example word for word that evening, in her journal, before her memory can soften it.

Grace, a day later, adds that Ayesha also says "Mm" in a flat voice while the person is still talking, which reads as impatience.

steps.label: Check against a recording
steps.text:
Grace says something similar: that Ayesha looks at her screen when problems come up. Two mirrors in different settings agreeing is worth taking seriously. Ayesha records her own camera feed in two stand-ups, after telling the team she is doing so for her own practice and will delete it. On the sound-off pass, she counts the sighs and the glances at the laptop. They are there, every time a problem is raised.

She also notices, on the recording, that she does it more on Mondays, when her inbox is fullest, which tells her something about when to be most careful.

steps.label: Change one thing
steps.text:
She chooses one change: when someone raises a problem, she closes her laptop lid, turns towards them and lets them finish, then says, "Thanks for raising it." She practises it for two weeks. She also tells the team, without detail, that she has had some feedback about how she responds to problems in stand-ups and is working on it, which is itself a signal that honesty is welcome.

She also asks Tom to tell her, before he leaves, if he sees the old habit come back.

She also writes the change on a sticky note on the edge of her monitor: "Laptop down. Turn. Let them finish."

steps.label: Close the loop
steps.text:
After two weeks, she goes back to Tom and Grace and asks: "A couple of weeks ago you mentioned I look at my laptop when people raise problems. I've been trying to stop. Have you noticed any difference?" Both say yes. Tom adds that two of the engineers mentioned it to him. A month later, one of the engineers who had stopped bringing her problems early brings her one on a Monday morning, and Ayesha closes her laptop.

She also writes the whole loop into her journal, from question to outcome, so that she can repeat it in six months.

moreFailures.title: Asking for feedback in public
moreFailures.body:
Asking for feedback in front of a group, as Leanne did when she read out her 360 comment at a team meeting, almost guarantees that nobody will say anything useful. The MUM effect, the reluctance to deliver bad news, is strongest when others are listening, because the person giving feedback risks embarrassing you and themselves in front of an audience. It is stronger still when you have power over the people in the room. Group requests for feedback tend to produce silence, safe generalities or, at best, a single brave person whose comment is then defended against in public. The chapter's method is private, one to one, with time to think. If you want feedback from a team, use anonymous channels for general views and private conversations with chosen mirrors for specifics, and never ask people to criticise you in front of each other.

If you need views from a whole team, use an anonymous survey for the general picture, and then ask individuals privately about specifics.

moreFailures.title: Cooling towards the messenger
moreFailures.body:
Some people receive feedback graciously in the moment and then, without quite meaning to, treat the person who gave it differently afterwards: a little cooler, a little less included, a little more likely to be passed over. The person giving the feedback notices, even if you do not, and so does everyone else who hears about it. Within a few months, your best mirror has stopped reflecting anything, and others have learned not to try. This is the slow version of arguing back, and it is even harder to see from the inside. If you ask someone for honest feedback, protect them afterwards. Thank them again later, tell them what you changed, and make a point of including them in the things that matter. The chapter's promise, "nothing you say will come back on you", has to be kept in your behaviour for months, not just in the moment.

A good test is whether your mirror would ask you for feedback in return. If they would, the loop is working.

moreFailures.title: Asking only people like you
moreFailures.body:
It is natural to ask for feedback from people you are comfortable with, and they are often people similar to you in age, background, role and style. But people like you share many of your blind spots. They may not notice that you talk over quieter colleagues, because they are not quiet; that you look past older people, because they are not older; or that your humour excludes people from different backgrounds, because it does not exclude them. This book has stressed throughout that the people least like you are the ones you are most likely to misread, and they are also the ones most likely to misread you, or to see what others miss. When you choose mirrors, include at least one person whose experience of you is likely to be different from your own, as Tim did when he asked a young youth worker at the back as well as a churchwarden at the front.

A simple way to start is to ask one person whose age, background or role is very different from yours the same question you asked your usual mirrors.

It also helps to ask your mirrors which of your habits they think other people notice most, which can reveal blind spots they share with you.

moreFailures.title: Asking for feedback you cannot use
moreFailures.body:
Feedback is most useful when it concerns something you can change, and least useful, sometimes harmful, when it concerns something you cannot. Asking people whether your face looks stern at rest, whether your accent is off-putting, or whether your height is intimidating may produce honest answers that you can do nothing with except worry. The chapter on video review in this part makes a similar point: change only the habits that are reliably misread, and use words to fill gaps that come from features. Ask instead about behaviours: what you do when someone disagrees, where your eyes go when you listen, what your hands do in tense moments. And do not ask too often. A mirror asked every week starts to feel like a judge, and begins to give answers that are either too kind or too sharp.

If you are unsure whether something can be changed, ask about what you do rather than what you are.

questions.q: Why will nobody tell me the truth about how I come across?
questions.a:
Mostly because telling someone bad news is uncomfortable, and people avoid it. Rosen and Tesser called this the MUM effect: people delay, soften or say nothing when the news is unwelcome, even when it is not their fault and even when the recipient needs it. Power makes it stronger, because the more people depend on your goodwill, the more they risk by being honest. And many people have learned, from you or from others, that honesty is met with argument. The result is that most of what others could tell you about your blind spot is filtered out before it reaches you. You can change this, but only deliberately: ask specific questions, privately, of people who have little to lose, and receive what they say without defending.

It also helps to notice whether you have ever argued with feedback, since people remember it for a long time.

questions.q: How can I ask for feedback without fishing for compliments?
questions.a:
Ask about a specific, observable behaviour, rather than about yourself in general. "How did I do?" and "How do I come across?" invite reassurance. "When I'm listening in meetings, what does my face do?" and "When someone disagrees with me, what do you notice first?" invite description. Ask for an example. Ask in private, and give the person time to think rather than expecting an answer on the spot. Tell them that you want the honest version and that nothing will come back on them. And when the answer comes, receive it as information, with thanks and one clarifying question, rather than as a verdict on who you are. People can tell the difference between someone looking for praise and someone looking for information.

It also helps to name the reason you are asking, such as a new role or a specific meeting, which makes the request feel practical rather than needy.

questions.q: What if the feedback seems unfair?
questions.a:
Notice which of Stone and Heen's three triggers it has touched. It may seem wrong, a truth trigger; you may resent the person giving it, a relationship trigger; or it may threaten your sense of who you are, an identity trigger, as Leanne's did. Each can make fair feedback feel unfair. Do not argue in the moment. Thank the person, ask for an example, and take it away to think. Then check it: against a recording, as Ayesha did, against a second mirror in a different setting, as Rajesh did, and against your journal. If two or three independent sources agree, take it seriously, even if it still feels wrong. If none does, it may genuinely say more about the person than about you.

And if you still think it is unfair after checking, you can thank the person and leave it there. Not all feedback needs acting on.

questions.q: How often should I ask for feedback?
questions.a:
Less often than you might think. One specific question to each of two or three mirrors, followed by a change and a return visit two weeks later, is a complete loop, and one loop every couple of months is plenty for most people. Asking too often wears out your mirrors and can make them feel like judges, which tends to produce answers that are either too gentle or too harsh. It can also make you self-conscious in the very situations you want to improve. The exception is when you are working on something specific and time-limited, such as a new role or a presentation: then a loop every few weeks for a short period makes sense, before you return to a slower rhythm.

It also helps to ask different mirrors at different times, so that no one person feels they are always the one you turn to.

questions.q: How should I give feedback about someone else's body language?
questions.a:
Only if they have asked, or if it genuinely matters to their work or wellbeing, and always privately. Keep it on the behaviour, not the person, as Kluger and DeNisi's findings suggest: describe what a camera would have recorded, with when and after what, as the Task, Not Self drill rehearses. "When Sam raised the budget, you looked at your phone for most of his answer" is usable; "You come across as dismissive" is not. Offer it as your observation, not a fact. Keep it to one thing. Avoid commenting on features people cannot change, such as their resting face or their accent. And leave room for them to disagree: they know their intentions, and you know only what you saw.

It also helps to ask whether they want it first: "I noticed something in that meeting. Would it be useful if I told you?"

questions.q: What if my partner is the only person who will be honest with me?
questions.a:
A partner can be a valuable mirror, because they see you often and usually wish you well. But they also have a stake in how you behave towards them, and they see you mainly in one setting, at home, which may not be the setting you most want to improve. Rajesh's experience with his mother shows how one close person's view can be both honest and misleading. Treat your partner's view as one mirror among several, and look for others: a colleague who is leaving, a peer in another team, a friend who sees you with other people. If you genuinely have no one else, a recording of yourself alone, reviewed with the method in the previous chapter, is a useful second view.

It also helps to ask your partner about a specific setting they see, such as how you are with your children, rather than about you in general.

And if your partner's view surprises you, ask them for one example, as you would anyone else.

watch.title: Want to get great at something? Get a coach
watch.notice: A surgeon on hiring a coach to watch him operate. Notice what an outside observer caught that years of experience had not.

reviewPrompt: Ask one of your honest mirrors one specific question about one observable habit, write down the answer word for word, and say only thank you.
